title: The Language of Wishing: How English Encodes Longing and Regret
paragraphs: Every language has a way of talking about things that are not real — desires unfulfilled, decisions regretted, lives unlived. In English, this space between reality and imagination is occupied by a set of constructions that linguists call "counterfactual" expressions. The most common of these are built around the verb "wish", the phrase "if only", and the conditional structures we use when we want to signal that we are speaking about something contrary to fact. Understanding how these structures work is not just a matter of grammar — it opens a window into the human experience of regret, hope, and speculation.

The verb "wish" in English is deceptively simple. When followed by a past tense verb, it expresses a desire about the present that cannot be satisfied: "I wish I lived closer to the city" means that the speaker does not, in fact, live close to the city. The past tense here does not refer to past time — it signals unreality. This grammatical "backward shift" is the same mechanism that underlies all conditional structures in English. When we say "If I were you, I would think carefully," the past tense "were" does not mean that the action happened yesterday; it means it is not happening now.

The expression "if only" works in the same way as "wish" but with greater emotional intensity. Compare these two sentences: "I wish I had studied harder" and "If only I had studied harder!" The second feels more urgent, more weighted with feeling. In spoken English, "if only" often appears without a main clause at all — "If only I had more time!" — and the listener understands the implied consequence: then things would be different. This "implicit consequence" structure is a feature of emotionally charged speech, where speakers omit what is obvious because the feeling itself carries the meaning.

English also has a range of expressions for imagining hypothetical situations more speculatively. "Supposing you had a second chance — what would you do differently?" "Imagine you could change one decision in your past." "What if everything had gone according to plan?" These phrases invite the listener or reader into a counterfactual world and ask them to think through the consequences. In academic writing, they appear as rhetorical devices; in everyday conversation, they are the currency of daydreaming and philosophical discussion.

Regret, as expressed in English, has a specific grammatical signature. The structure "should have + past participle" points to an obligation that was not fulfilled: "I should have called her earlier." The structure "need not have + past participle" expresses an unnecessary action that was performed: "I need not have worried — everything turned out fine." Both structures use the perfect infinitive to locate the regretted action firmly in the past, distinguishing it from present or future states. This precision allows English speakers to be extremely specific about the timing and nature of their regrets.

An interesting feature of counterfactual language is its social function. When we say "I wish things were different" or "If only the situation were less complicated," we are not merely describing an internal state — we are also performing a social act. We are signalling humility (acknowledging that things are not within our control), expressing solidarity (we wish things were better for everyone), or managing expectations (implying that we would act differently if circumstances allowed). Linguists call these "face-saving" strategies, and they are an important part of polite English communication.

Learning to use counterfactual language confidently is a mark of genuine B1 fluency. It requires not just knowing the grammar rules — though those matter — but also developing a sensitivity to the emotional register of different expressions. "I wish" is neutral and widely applicable. "If only" is more intense and often signals genuine regret. "Supposing" and "imagine" are more playful and intellectual. Mastering these distinctions allows learners to express the full range of human longing, speculation, and reflection in English.

task1Items.correct: An obligation that was not fulfilled; regret about past action
